In our commitment to open town meeting, Hingham remains true to a wonderful tradition – a tradition that allows each registered voter to play a pivotal role in the governance of the town and to do so with “voice and vote”. Town meeting is not only a gathering of citizens to consider matters of common concern; it is the legislative body of the town. As such, the meeting must be conducted in a fair and open manner and in accordance with the Town Bylaws, as well as traditions that we have followed in Hingham town meetings for many years. Several matters of procedure are summarized below.  An article in the warrant states a question for the town meeting to answer. A motion is a proposed answer to the question and must be within the scope of the article. An article (once published in the warrant) may not be amended, but a motion may be amended by vote of the meeting. All motions must be seconded.  If the Advisory Committee is recommending an affirmative motion under an article, its motion will be received as the main motion under the article. A voter may propose to amend this motion, either to change it in part or to substitute a whole new motion (sometimes called a "substitute motion"). In any such case, the proposed amendment will be taken up and voted on first and then the main motion, as it may have been amended, will be acted upon.  If the Advisory Committee is recommending no action under an article and a voter offers an affirmative motion, the voter's motion will be received as the main motion under the article. Such a motion is likewise subject to amendment.  All motions and proposed amendments involving the expenditure of money must be in writing. So must all other motions and proposed amendments unless they are so brief and simple as to be easily understood when stated orally (e.g., motion for the previous question, motion to adjourn). Voters are welcome to seek the assistance of counsel for the Town in preparing motions or proposed amendments.  Limits on speaking: No one may speak on any subject for more than six (6) minutes for the first time or for more than three (3) minutes for the second time. No one may speak more than twice on any question unless all others who have not spoken on the question shall have spoken if they desire to do so and unless leave of the meeting is first obtained. A person may speak more than twice, but only to make a brief correction of an error in or misunderstanding of his or her previous statement, including brief answers to questions from the floor (addressed through the Moderator).  In addressing the meeting, a speaker shall confine his or her remarks to the matter before the meeting.  Persons who are not registered voters of the Town may be admitted to the meeting as guests by the Moderator. A guest of the meeting may be granted permission to address the meeting by majority vote.  The purpose of the motion for the previous question is to end discussion and have an immediate vote on the pending question. The motion is not debatable and requires a majority vote for adoption. The Moderator will decline to accept a motion for the previous question if 2 other voters are seeking recognition and if both sides have not had a fair opportunity to be heard. The Moderator will accept the motion for the previous question if it appears that both sides have been heard and the discussion is becoming repetitious.  Voting procedures: All votes are taken in the first instance by voice vote. If the Moderator is in doubt as to the results or if seven (7) voters rise and express doubt as to the result declared by the Moderator, a standing vote is taken, except that a ballot vote is taken (instead of a standing vote) if either the Advisory Committee or fifty (50) voters promptly call for a ballot vote. As a ballot vote takes considerable time, our practice has been not to request a ballot vote in the absence of compelling reasons.  At a Special Town Meeting, no money may be appropriated for any purpose if the Advisory Committee recommends against the appropriation, except by a two-thirds vote of the meeting.  No vote may be reconsidered except after a two-thirds vote on a motion to reconsider such vote. The Town acknowledges that the MSBA’s grant program is a non-entitlement, discretionary program based on need, as determined by the MSBA, and any Project costs the Town incurs in excess of any grant approved by and received from the MSBA shall be the sole responsibility of the Town. Any grant that the Town may receive from the MSBA for the Project shall not exceed the lesser (1) thirty six, and eighty-nine hundredths’ percent (36.89%) of eligible, approved Project costs, as determined by the MSBA, or (2) the total maximum grant amount determined by the MSBA, or act on anything relating thereto? (Inserted at the request of the 2025 School Building Committee) COMMENT: This Article seeks authorization to fund the replacement of the roof systems at South Elementary School (“South”). The existing roof systems are of varying ages and conditions and have required repairs and maintenance over time; much of the system has reached the end of its useful life. Recently, water infiltration from ice dams required an emergency response. The proposed Project is being developed in conjunction with the Massachusetts School Building Authority (“MSBA”) Accelerated Repair Program. Background South was constructed in 1948. The school roof is approximately 57,000 square feet. The building underwent an extensive expansion and renovation in 1998 at which point the school’s roofing systems were also completely replaced. Since that time the district has maintained it mainly through targeted repairs, with an emergency repair performed as recently as summer 2025. A 2022 study performed by Habeeb & Associates, the Town’s professional consultants, found that most of the 13 sections of the roofing (and the associated drainage fixtures) needed repair, and noted that the roof systems had exceeded their 20-year warranty. The report further noted that all roofing sections were approaching the end of their standard 25-year life expectancy and thus should be replaced in the near to intermediate term. As part of this roof Project Habeeb & Associates has been contracted to conduct a peer review of all design materials being submitted through the MSBA process. 2025 Annual Town Meeting authorized $320,000 for a schematic design study for the anticipated roofing systems replacement. The Town was subsequently accepted into the MSBA Accelerated Repair Program, and an Owner’s Project Manager was selected by the MSBA. All six public school buildings are actively required to accommodate current and projected student enrollment, based on Hingham Public Schools' facility evaluations and long-term planning. Overall enrollment is experiencing an increase, and over the next 10 years, elementary enrollments are projected by New England School Development Council (“NESDEC”) to increase by 304 students. 5 Building Study and Design Process To-Date Following the Town's acceptance into the MSBA's Accelerated Repair Program, the Project's design consultant, Gale Associates (“Gale”), was engaged to evaluate the roof and develop a schematic design. The April, 2026, evaluation included a visual assessment of the roofing and flashing; limited exploratory openings; hazardous-material sampling; an infrared drone survey; and a structural feasibility study. A related Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (“MAAB”) evaluation was subsequently conducted in early May, 2026. A whole roof system assessment study found that many portions of the South roof sub-structure are sound. Original timber framing installed in 1948, does not meet current snow-load Building Code (“Code”) requirements, and requires structural augmentation. In addition, several framing members in the 1998 expansion are very close to their maximum capacity (98%), and Gale recommended structural augmentation for that portion of the building as well. The remaining portions of the roof framing and decks are generally capable of supporting current code-required loads, although several framing members require reinforcement due to insufficient capacity for the additional load of future solar panels. Although the Town is not obligated to install solar panels, under the MSBA grant program, the roof structure must have a designated solar-ready area with sufficient capacity to support solar panels. The evaluation further found that most of the asphalt shingle and low-slope membrane roofing areas are more than 20 years old and showing signs of deterioration, including damaged shingles, poor-condition roof coatings, previous repairs related to water infiltration, and deteriorated flashing, sealants, and masonry. While the existing standing-seam metal roofing is generally serviceable, replacing it as part of the Project would provide a uniform, warrantable, and betterinsulated roof system. Limited hazardous-material testing found no asbestos in the samples collected, although additional testing will be required as the project progresses. Lead-based paint was identified on a roof truss, and the Project budget includes an allowance for potential abatement of both asbestos and lead. Lower-cost coating and overlay options for the existing roofing systems were also considered. These options were not recommended because they would not address the underlying deterioration and would require continued maintenance and repairs. The study concluded that continued patching and repairs would not provide a durable, long-term solution. The recommended approach is to replace the roof systems and address related flashing, masonry and drainage problems at the same time. Following Gale’s review, roof-covering options and cost comparisons were reviewed with Hingham Public Schools and the 2025 School Building Committee (“SBC”) in public meetings in June 2026. The SBC voted to proceed with PVC membrane roofing on the low-slope areas and standing-seam metal panels on the steep-slope areas. That direction, combined with findings on the age and condition of the existing systems, culminated in a Schematic Design submitted to the MSBA on August 27, 2026, and revised on September 18, 2026; this Schematic Design is the basis for the scope and cost estimate presented in this Article. Proposed Project The proposed Project will replace the existing roofing systems down to the roof decks, with the decks inspected and repaired as needed. The work will include new low-slope and steep-slope 6 roofing systems, along with related improvements to roof edges, flashing, drainage, gutters and downspouts, and rooftop equipment. The Project will also include reinforcement of selected roof framing and related interior work to meet current Code requirements and support potential future solar installation in the designated areas. Because the proposed roof assemblies will be thicker than the existing assemblies, related modifications will be required to drainage, roof-edge and flashing systems, as well as portions of the masonry. The work will also include masonry repairs, replacement of deteriorated sealants, and replacement or modification of existing roof ladders and other roof-access components. Because the Project cost exceeds 30% of the building’s assessed value, the Project must address accessibility throughout the building, not just in areas directly affected by the roof work. Thus, the Project will include accessibility improvements identified through a review of the school for compliance with applicable MAAB requirements. The preliminary scope includes modifications to toilet-room accessories, door hardware, portions of the exterior ramp and sidewalk, handrails, signage, vestibule flooring, doors and thresholds, and water coolers. Proposed Project Cost Based on the current Schematic Design, the total Project cost is $8,576,727, an increase from the $5,400,000 estimate presented at the 2025 Annual Town Meeting. The study and evaluation of the existing roof identified additional needs, most notably the augmentation of the wood-framed roof and structural steel trusses. The expanded scope was not contemplated in the previous estimate and has been incorporated into the current Project cost. Furthermore, Project costs have increased significantly over the past two years, reflecting continued construction cost escalation and broader inflationary pressures affecting labor and materials. MUNICIPAL FINANCE TERMS APPROPRIATION – An authorization by the Town Meeting to make obligations and payments from the treasury for a specific purpose. ASSESSED VALUATION – A valuation set upon real or personal property by the Board of Assessors as a basis for levying taxes. BETTERMENT – A betterment assessment is a charge for the cost of public improvements, which benefit a limited area, against real estate situated in such. BAN – “Bond Anticipatory Note”. Short term borrowing done in advance of long term borrowing via issuance of a BOND. BANs are issued to be able to fund a project while waiting to go to formal bonding. BOND – A loan, typically over a year in maturity. BOND AUTHORIZATION – The amount of money the Town Meeting approves for borrowing for a specific purpose. BOND / BAN PREMIUM – Funds paid to the Town by financial institutions as commissions on the sale of the Town’s BONDS or BANs. These premiums are allowed under the Massachusetts Municipal Act of 2016 under Chapter 44, section 20 to be used to fund similar Capital Projects to the projects funded by the original BOND/BAN. BOND ISSUE – Generally, the sale of a certain number of bonds at one time by a governmental unit. CAPITAL BUDGET – A plan of proposed capital outlays and the means of financing them for the current fiscal period. CAPITAL OUTLAY – An expenditure for the purchase of property or equipment and for the construction or renovation of a facility and infrastructure. CHERRY SHEET – A form showing all state and county charges and reimbursements to the town as certified by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue. DEBT SERVICE – Payment of interest and repayment of principal to holders of the town’s debt instruments. ENTERPRISE FUND – Financing of services where all or most of the costs are paid for by users. ENTERPRISE RETAINED EARNINGS – If during a fiscal year an Enterprise fund produces a surplus, such surplus shall be kept in a separate account called “retained earnings”. The Department of Revenue then certifies that surplus as an available fund which can be used for: 1. operating costs to offset the need to increase user charges, 2. to fund capital improvements, 3. to reimburse General Fund to the extent the General Fund has funded a particular service in prior years, or 4. to fund Enterprise Fund revenue deficits. FISCAL YEAR - A 12-month period, commencing on July 1, to which the annual budget applies. (Abbreviated as "FY".) FREE CASH - The excess of assets over liabilities, minus uncollected taxes of prior years, also referred to as "available cash". The amount is certified annually by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue. Free Cash may be appropriated by vote of a town meeting. GENERAL FUND - The major town owned fund which is created with town receipts and which is charged with expenditures payable from such revenues. GRANT - A contribution of assets by one governmental unit or other organization to another. Typically, these contributions are made to local governments from the state and federal government. Grants are usually made for specific purposes. LEVY LIMIT - The amount of dollars a Town can raise by taxation under Proposition 2 1/2. LINE-ITEM BUDGET - A format of budgeting which organizes costs by type of expenditure. Such as expenses, equipment, and salaries. OVERLAY - The overlay is the amount raised by the Assessors to be used for potential abatement of property taxes. The Overlay Surplus is the portion of each year's overlay account no longer required to cover property tax abatements. PROPERTY TAX LEVY - The amount produced by multiplying the assessed valuation of property by the tax rate. The tax rate is expressed "per thousand dollars" of assessed valuation. RESERVE FUND - Money set aside by Town Meeting to be allocated by the Advisory Board for extraordinary and unforeseen expenditures. REVOLVING FUND (Ch.44, Sec. 53E 1/2) - A Town may annually authorize the use of a revolving fund by accounting for separately the receipts received from a particular service or program and expend from such fund for providing such service or program without appropriation. STABILIZATION FUND - A special account which is invested until used and can only be utilized by town meeting appropriation. MOTION MOVE to appoint John Canal, Georgia Jones, and Nicolas LeVangle, to the position of patrol officer effective October 13, 2026 contingent upon passage of the Police Academy, passage of a physical abilities, medical, and physiological exam, and a one-year probationary period. 6. 7:10 Discuss and Vote FY28 Budget Guideline Discussions The FY28 budget continues to present significant financial challenges, with pressure coming from health insurance, collective bargaining and step increases, departmental operating costs, capital requirements, and competing demands for Free Cash. While the Town-Wide Financial Plan (TWFP) provides the starting framework for FY28, several significant assumptions remain unresolved and will need to be monitored as the budget develops. Health Insurance and Fixed Costs Health insurance remains one of the largest variables in the FY28 budget. At this stage, the Town does not yet have a formal trend analysis on which to base a revised projection. The current TWFP therefore continues to carry an 8% increase for medical health insurance and 5% for all other insurance (dental, life insurance, accident, hospital indemnity, eyemed). There is reason to believe actual FY27 medical claims experience may improve. Coverage for GLP-1 medications has been significantly reduced, which is expected to reduce claims costs in FY28. However, until sufficient claims experience and trend information are available, staff is not recommending that the Town reduce the existing TWFP assumption. The health insurance projection should continue to be reviewed as additional claims information becomes available, which likely is start of December. Personnel Services and Collective Bargaining Personnel costs remain a significant component of the FY28 budget, particularly as the Town continues negotiations with its municipal and school collective bargaining units. The draft guidelines therefore identify departments with open collective bargaining agreements separately rather than assigning a fixed personnel services percentage before those negotiations are completed. FY28 also represents a 52.4-week payroll year, a circumstance that occurs approximately once every seven years. As a result, personnel budgets will experience an additional year-over-year increase simply from the additional payroll obligation. This increase occurs before accounting for COLAs, merit increases, contractual wage adjustments, staffing changes or other compensation costs and is reflected in the departmental personnel service guidelines. For non-union employees, based on the Select Board's discussion last week and the recommendation of the Human Resources Board, the CFO and Executive Director are recommending a 2% COLA for FY28. In addition, the recommendation continues the $300,000 Merit Pay Plan pool for eligible employees and includes $25,000 for other compensation adjustments. The recommended approach provides a consistent general wage adjustment while preserving the Town's performance-based compensation structure. The $25,000 adjustment allocation provides limited capacity to address individual compensation issues that may arise during the year without incorporating those costs into the general COLA or Merit Pay Plan. The departmental personnel guidelines reflect these assumptions, the 52.4-week payroll year, and known staffing or department-specific circumstances. Departments with open collective bargaining agreements—including Police, Fire, DPW, Facilities Management and the Library— remain identified as Union Negotiations pending resolution of those agreements. Operating Expense Budget Pressures The draft guidelines attempt to hold most departmental operating expense budgets level while recognizing specific costs that cannot reasonably be absorbed within a 0% guideline. Information Technology is recommended at an 8% expense guideline, together with approximately $100,000 for the Munis increase and $25,000 for applicant tracking software, reflecting continued increases in cybersecurity, licensing, telephone and enterprise software costs. Facilities Management is recommended at 5% for expenses, with an additional lease-related increase identified in the draft. Utility costs remain an additional unknown because MLP and natural gas increases have not yet been finalized. National Grid could be increased for both commodity and transmission up to 10%. Other identified pressures include a contractual Audit Committee increase, increased hybrid cruiser costs for Police, Library licensing and subscription costs, a projected $75,000–$100,000 trash contract increase for DPW, new transportation contract costs for the Schools, and a 6% Workers' Compensation increase associated with the recent valuation. Capital Financing and Cash Capital The preliminary FY28 capital model presents an additional challenge. Staff is recommending that cash capital be modeled at 6% of recurring revenues, which is below the minimum range established in the Town's existing capital financing framework. Even at 6%, based on current projections, approximately $1.3 million in capital reductions will be required. This means that the 6% recommendation should not be viewed as creating additional budget flexibility. Rather, it already assumes that projects currently contemplated in the capital program will need to be reduced, deferred or funded through another source. Staff will work through the capital program to identify options for achieving the required reduction and bring those choices back to the Board as the capital and operating budgets develop. All capital submittals are not due until November 20th for FY28. Free Cash and Additional Capital Needs Free Cash is likely to play an important role in the FY28 financial plan, but it is important to consider the FY28 discussion in the context of the significant uses of Free Cash already made or planned during FY27. Free Cash has been identified for the following FY27 purposes: • • • • Comprehensive Plan – $350,000 Library LED – $325,000 School AC Design – $1,423,400 School AC Design – Accelerated – $170,200 (SC Request) Free Cash has been identified for the following FY28 TWFP purposes: • • • • • Snow and Ice Supplemental – $1,000,000 Operating Budget Balance – $2,000,000 (Best Case Scenario) School Facilities Strategic Planning – $200,000 Fire Station Feasibility – $750,000 (2 Sites is approximately $1.6M) Pre-School Feasibility – $500,000 These uses total approximately $6.72 million. Looking ahead to FY28, additional demands on Free Cash are already emerging. In addition to projects currently contemplated in the TWFP, Facilities Management has provided preliminary estimates for: • • • $1,114,000 – Middle School Roof Interim Repairs $850,000 – Bates Parking Lot and Site Renovation (ROM estimate; engineering/design is underway) $405,000 – FMD/Land Use Lease Cost – Accommodations These preliminary FY28 needs total an additional $2.369 million. Taken together, the identified FY27 uses and these preliminary FY28 needs represent approximately $9.09 million in Free Cash demands, before considering any additional At the same time, a Citizen Petition proposes an additional expenditure of Free Cash ($7.8M). Any significant additional appropriation from Free Cash must therefore be considered in the context of both the Town's available Free Cash balance and the uses of Free Cash that may otherwise be necessary to support the FY28 budget and capital program. This is particularly important because Free Cash is a finite, non-recurring resource that must also be replenished each year. Using Free Cash for one purpose necessarily reduces the amount available for other one-time capital needs, budget balancing, reserves, or other financial priorities. The Board will need to consider these competing uses collectively rather than evaluating individual Free Cash requests in isolation. Preliminary Departmental Guidelines The attached draft reflects department-specific recommendations based on the requests presented through the All-Board process and the cost drivers currently known. Most departmental expense budgets are being held at 0%, while targeted increases are recommended where contractual, utility, technology or other identifiable costs make a level-funded budget unrealistic. Personnel guidelines have similarly been adjusted based on known circumstances. Departments with open collective bargaining agreements are identified separately because assigning a percentage guideline before negotiations are completed could create an inaccurate budget assumption. The Schools' preliminary FY28 personnel guideline is 3.4%, reflecting the impact of the 52.4week payroll schedule on the TWFP percentage. Schools continue to be in negotiations as well. The Schools have also identified additional potential cost pressures, including new transportation contracts and the proposed statewide MassCore graduation requirements. While the Healey administration has recommended implementation on MassCore beginning with incoming ninthgrade students in the 2027–2028 school year, legislation establishing the statewide requirement has not been enacted. The potential financial implications for Wellesley remain uncertain and will need to be evaluated as the State's implementation requirements and timelines become clearer. Guideline Framing Given the combined pressures on the FY28 budget, the recommended guidelines are intended to establish a disciplined starting point rather than predetermine the final budget. Departments should continue to prioritize existing core services and contractual obligations, identify opportunities for efficiencies, and distinguish unavoidable cost increases from program enhancements. New programs, positions or service expansions should be considered in the context of the Town's overall financial capacity and should not be assumed simply because they are included within a departmental request. The more significant FY28 challenge will be balancing the operating budget, capital program and Free Cash strategy together. The current plan already assumes a capital level that will require approximately $1.3 million in reductions, while additional Facilities needs and other potential Free Cash appropriations could further constrain the Town's ability to use Free Cash as originally contemplated in the TWFP. The draft guidelines are therefore presented as a starting point for Select Board consideration. The Select Board is being asked to approve a new five-year Cable Television Renewal License with Verizon New England Inc. The Select Board serves as the Town’s Issuing Authority for cable television licenses pursuant to M.G.L. Chapter 166A. Verizon’s current five-year renewal license became effective November 6, 2021, and the proposed renewal would take effect November 6, 2026 and continue through November 5, 2031. The renewal authorizes Verizon to continue providing cable television service in Wellesley and establishes the terms governing service, Public, Educational and Governmental (PEG) access, financial support to the Town, customer service, reporting, and other license obligations. Town staff, Wellesley Media Corp Executive Director James Joyce and cable counsel Bill August have negotiated the renewal with Verizon. The proposed agreement generally maintains the significant municipal and PEG benefits contained in the current license while updating several provisions to reflect changes in technology, federal requirements and the cable television market. Key Municipal Benefits and Changes PEG Operating Support – Maintained at 5% The most significant ongoing financial benefit is preserved. Verizon will continue to provide annual PEG Access/Cable-Related Support equal to 5% of Verizon’s annual gross cable revenues in Wellesley, paid quarterly. These funds may be used by the Town for cable-related purposes and to support personnel, operating and other costs associated with PEG programming. The methodology for calculating revenues from bundled cable and non-cable services is also continued under the renewal. PEG Capital Funding – $142,395 The current license provided $150,000 in PEG capital funding, paid in three $50,000 installments. The proposed renewal provides $142,395, paid in three installments of $47,465 during the first three years of the license. While this represents a $7,605 reduction from the current license, the modest reduction should be viewed in the context of a significant decline in Verizon’s Wellesley subscriber base—from approximately 3,107 subscribers when the current license began in 2021 to 2,218 at the end of 2025, a decline of nearly 30%. The negotiated amount is based on the same capital funding structure used with Comcast: an amount equivalent to 0.45% of Verizon’s current gross revenues, converted to a fixed annual dollar amount so that it will not decline if Verizon’s revenues continue to decrease, plus an additional $9,800 annually despite Verizon having fewer subscribers than Comcast. The resulting five-year commitment is $142,395, only $7,605 less than the prior agreement. Importantly, the Town also negotiated payment of the full five-year commitment during the first three years of the license, providing the Town with the benefit of receiving the capital funding earlier and reducing the risk associated with future subscriber or revenue declines. The renewal also expressly provides that the PEG capital grant is separate from the 5% operating support and license fees, and that equipment purchased with the grant will be owned by the Town and/or its designated PEG provider. PEG Channels and High-Definition Capability – Enhanced The agreement continues Verizon’s obligation to provide the Town with three standard-definition PEG channels and one high-definition PEG channel. The renewal provides additional flexibility by allowing the Town or its PEG Access Designee to request that some or all of the existing standard-definition channels be replaced with high-definition channels. Verizon must make each requested replacement HD channel available within 270 days. HD programming may be provided in either 720p or 1080i format. PEG Interconnection and Equipment – Additional Town Protection Verizon will continue its PEG interconnection with Town equipment at 485 Washington Street. The new agreement provides an additional protection for the Town by clarifying that the Town will not be responsible for Verizon-side upgrade or repair costs when the work is necessary to comply with applicable law or to correct a defect in equipment or facilities for which Verizon is responsible, including issues affecting video or audio quality. Cable Service to Public Buildings The renewal continues to identify the Town and school buildings eligible for cable service in Exhibit A, including Town Hall, Police and Fire Stations, libraries, DPW facilities and public schools. The provisions governing complimentary service have been revised to address the FCC's treatment of free or discounted municipal cable service under the federal franchise-fee cap. Existing service to designated buildings will continue until Verizon implements the applicable federal requirements following the notice process contained in the agreement. PEG Administration The renewal replaces the more limited reference to an “Access Corporation” with the broader term “PEG Access Designee.” This allows the Select Board to designate either a nonprofit/noncommercial entity or a municipal department to manage PEG channels, facilities, funding and programming, providing the Town with greater flexibility in how PEG services are administered. This was done to codify the historic use of homes on Cape Cod as vacation rentals in response to 2021 case law that questioned this type of use unless expressly allowed in the Zoning Bylaw. The original STR bylaw was prepared expeditiously to ensure continued economic benefits and revenues to the Town from the short-term rental tax. STRs are a vital revenue stream for the Town, bringing in over $2.375 Million in Fiscal Year 26, with 75% going towards funding our wastewater program to improve our estuaries and water quality. As the bylaw was developed in an expedited manner, a sunset clause was included in the bylaw to allow time for further studies or analysis, with the STR provisions currently expiring on November 30, 2026, unless amended at Town Meeting. Subsequent studies conducted included a detailed Short-Term Rental Report by UMass Donahue Institute dated February 2026. This study analyzed demographics, the housing market, STRs in Yarmouth, impacts and benefits of STRs, reviewed existing regulations and identified potential new regulations. This study was presented to the Select Board at their March 3, 2026 meeting and STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #6 – October 14, 2026 Page 4 of 5 recommended a multi-faceted strategy. In addition to looking at various ways to incentivize yearround housing, the study discussed tailoring regulations to inhibit future commercialization of STRs, strengthen compliance, and further address quality of life issues. The Planning Board used this study to start developing draft language and holding public meetings to garner community input. Some key provisions and modifications contained within the General Bylaw include:  further restrictions on types of dwellings that can be used as a STR  further clarifications on occupancy, parking, noise, and type of rentals  identification of specific information to be included within all STR listings, and  enhanced penalties and enforcement including the potential revocation of a Rental Occupancy Certificate related to verified violations. OWNER – Any person, corporation, LLC, trust or other entity that, alone, or severally with others, directly or indirectly, has legal or equitable title or beneficial interest in any dwelling unit. OPERATOR – A person or entity who is designated by an Owner to be responsible for the dayto-day operations of the Short-Term Rental and who serves as the local 24-hour emergency contact person with the Town of Yarmouth. An Owner may also be an Operator provided they are available 24 hours a day during the rental period to address operational issues at the Short-Term Rental. SHORT-TERM RENTALS (STR) - defined as owner-occupied, tenant-occupied or non-owner occupied residential property including, but not limited to, an apartment unit, house, cottage, condominium or a furnished accommodation that is not a hotel, motel, boarding or lodging house, or guesthouse, inn or bed and breakfast establishment, where at least one room or unit is rented to an occupant or occupants for 1-31 consecutive days at a time. STRs are characterized as transient in nature and not rented to the same occupant month to month. TIME SHARE, FRACTIONAL AND INTERVAL OWNERSHIP UNIT - Any Dwelling Unit which is owned by a limited liability company, corporation, partnership, or other joint ownership structure in which unrelated persons or entities own, sell, purchase or otherwise, for consideration, create or acquire any divided property interest including co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are subject to, or subsequently bound by any agreement limiting the right or functional ability of interest holders or their designees to occupy or use the property to their respective interests or any other agreement which limits interest holders’ or their designees’ use of the property to fractional reservations through stay limitations of any duration. Ineligible Units. The following are not eligible to be rented as STRs. 1. Dwellings designated as income restricted or which are subject to affordability covenants or restrictions. 2.
